a: In September 2023 a social-media trend revealed that a remarkable number of men think about the Roman Empire daily — some several times a day. We felt the underlying question deserved a proper answer, on a schedule. So every morning at 06:00 UTC a GitHub Actions workflow checks whether the Roman Empire is back, recomputes the counters, pulls the latest Wikipedia pageview data, and republishes this page.

Our criteria, none of which is currently met:

  • ☐ A functioning Senate sitting in Rome (the Curia Julia is still standing; it is a museum)
  • ☐ At least one legion — roughly 4,800 legionaries; re-enactors and the Swiss Guard do not count
  • ☐ Latin as the working language of government (Vatican City is 0.49 km² and does not count)
  • ☐ A recognised Augustus, acclaimed by army or Senate
  • ☐ Control of mare nostrum — all of it
  • ☐ Bread and circuses (circuses must be chariot-grade)

Partial credit is not available. The Roman Empire is a binary system.

q: Which fall are you counting from?
a: Both. The main counter starts on 4 September 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and the Western Empire ended. The second starts on 29 May 1453, when Constantinople fell and the Eastern Empire — which called itself Roman to the very end — went with it. For the day counts the Julian dates are converted to the proleptic Gregorian calendar (5 September 476 and 7 June 1453) so the arithmetic is exact.

q: What about the Holy Roman Empire, the Ottomans, or Russia?
a: Claimants, not continuations. The Holy Roman Empire (800/962–1806) was, per Voltaire, neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. The Ottoman sultans styled themselves Kayser-i Rûm until 1922; Moscow called itself the Third Rome until 1917. All of them are tracked under Successor-claim watch. Active claims: zero.

q: How is the Roman Thought Index calculated?
a: Daily pageviews by human users for six English Wikipedia articles — Roman Empire, Ancient Rome, Roman Republic, Julius Caesar, Fall of the Western Roman Empire, and Byzantine Empire — summed, via the public Wikimedia REST API. The headline figure is the most recent complete day; the level compares it with the trailing 30-day mean. It measures attention, not legions.

q: How does the Roman date work?
a: Romans counted backwards, inclusively, to three fixed points in each month: the Kalends (1st), the Nones (5th, or 7th in March, May, July and October), and the Ides (13th, or 15th in those same months). So 21 August is ante diem XII Kalendas Septembres — the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. Years are given ab urbe condita (A.U.C.), from Varro's founding date of 753 BC. Consuls are not listed because there have been none since Basilius in AD 541.

Because if a service ran from 21 April 753 BC to 29 May 1453 and has been down ever since, the honest metric is uptime. Rome currently scores about 79% over its lifetime — respectable, but short of four nines, and the incident has been open for more than fifteen centuries without a postmortem.

A human with a GitHub account and a robot that checks every morning. The source, the data and the update script are on GitHub. Corrections and additions — books, films, resources, dates — are welcome as pull requests; all content lives in plain JSON files under data/.

q: Is this affiliated with the Roman Empire?
a: No. The Roman Empire is not currently accepting affiliations.
